The parties are a consequence of the real problem. Our voting system, first past the post, is increasingly something primarily used by the third world and a handful of countries that are using it to maintain a political stranglehold on their peoples. It is the system where if 4 people run with 26%, 25%, 25%, 24% then the person with 26% immediately wins the whole election and gets 100% of the representation. It naturally leads to two parties as the 26% approaches the 24% guy and says "Hey I know we don't agree on pretty much anything, but if we don't team up there's a good chance neither of us get any representation at all." The two 25% fellows see what's happening and do the exact same thing.

This is the reason you somehow have neocons, libertarians, and christian fundamentalists all jammed into one party. It also leads to completely fake politicians. Many of the views within the party are completely self contradictory so they're forced to draw on a handful of issues they can unite their followers on through agreement or apathy towards said issue. It's the reason, for instance, that even though Roe vs Wade is now going on half a century old, we still use it as a contemporary political issue. It's also the reason our representatives are so incredibly fake. How many people look at Hillary or Jeb and think, "Yeah.. I think this person really stands for me and what I believe in." It's going to be pretty close to 0. Their entire political existence is based on simply being less offensive than the alternative.

I'd really love to vote for Trumpey Donders but I don't want to waste my vote. I think the only person that can realistically win Hitt Clintoney so I'm going vote for xe since xe's certainly less awful than the alternative of Clit Hittoney!" This ability to force people to vote against their own self interest is unique to first past the post. It basically ensures that whichever parties are in power and can most effectively control the media will win the election. It's also the reason the only thing that actually tends to correlate strongly with results in US elections is money spent.

Depends what you mean by "useful". But they're certainly inevitable. They have arisen independently in thousands of different democratic systems, and if you ban them then they will come back in some informal way that skirts whatever law you passed to ban them.

Elected representatives, and those standing for election, will inevitably form alliances, which over time will harden into formal political parties. And individuals will usually tend to vote for a member of an alliance over a completely independent person, since (a) they can get more done, and (b) an alliance is just as likely to follow your own personal views as some random individual, and (c) it takes too long to research every random individual, but I know the basic ideology I'm going to get out of a major party.
